title: Functional progressions
description: Memorize tonic, predominant, and dominant jobs, the core progressions, and how blues and cadences reuse them.

cards.front: Name the three harmonic functions and what each does.
cards.back: Tonic (T): home, rest, arrival. Predominant (PD): departure and preparation. Dominant (D): tension that wants to return home.

cards.front: Which diatonic chords typically fill T, PD, and D?
cards.back: Tonic: I; vi often substitutes; iii is a weaker tonic substitute. Predominant: IV and ii. Dominant: V, V7, and vii°.

cards.front: What is the classic function order, and is it a rule?
cards.back: T to PD to D to T. It is a tendency, not a law. Popular music, blues, and modal writing often use other orders.

cards.front: Do functions describe what a chord is made of?
cards.back: No. Functions describe what a chord tends to do in a key, not its quality. Context decides the job.

cards.front: In C major, why do ii and IV share predominant function?
cards.back: ii is D F A and IV is F A C. They share F and A, and both contain scale degree 4 (F), which wants to fall to E.

cards.front: In C major, why do V and vii° share dominant function?
cards.back: V is G B D and vii° is B D F. They share B and D. Both contain degree 7 (B), which wants to rise to C.

cards.front: Why can vi stand in for I?
cards.back: In C, I is C E G and vi is A C E. They share C and E, so vi can replace I without a large change in sound.

cards.front: Spell I IV V I in C and label the functions.
cards.back: C F G C. Tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic.

cards.front: Spell ii V I in C major, and how do the roots move?
cards.back: Dm7 G7 Cmaj7. Roots move down by a fifth each time.

cards.front: In Dm7 G7 Cmaj7, how do the guide tones move?
cards.back: The seventh of Dm7 (C) falls a half step to the third of G7 (B). The third of Dm7 (F) is the seventh of G7 and holds, then falls a half step to the third of Cmaj7 (E). The B can stay as the major seventh of Cmaj7.

cards.front: Spell minor ii V i in C minor. Where does the B in G7 come from?
cards.back: Dm7♭5 G7 Cm7. The G7 carries B, borrowed from harmonic minor.

cards.front: State a common 12-bar blues form with seventh chords (bars 1–12).
cards.back: I7 I7 (or IV7) I7 I7 | IV7 IV7 I7 I7 | V7 IV7 I7 I7 (or V7).

cards.front: In a blues, why is “a 7 chord is always V” misleading?
cards.back: I7 and IV7 are dominant-quality chords that are not functioning as dominants of the key. Neither is tension waiting to resolve. The V7 in bars 9 and 12 does lead back to I7.

cards.front: What is a retrogression, and where is it common?
cards.back: V to IV. Common in rock and blues. It sounds like a deliberate step away from the dominant, not a mistake.

cards.front: What does V to vi do? What does IV to I do?
cards.back: V to vi is a deceptive move: dominant expectation, tonic-substitute arrival. IV to I is a gentle plagal close.

cards.front: In G, spell I V vi IV, I vi IV V, I vi ii V, and I ♭VII IV I.
cards.back: G D Em C; G Em C D; Gmaj7 Em7 Am7 D7; G F C G. The last uses a borrowed ♭VII.

cards.front: In G, what open-position shapes play I IV V I and I vi IV V?
cards.back: I IV V I: G 320003, C x32010, D xx0232, G. I vi IV V: G, Em 022000, C, D.

cards.front: What open shapes play ii V I in G?
Give the string-5/6 shells for Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 and their notes.
cards.back: Dm7 x5x56x (D C F). G7 3xx46x (G B F). Cmaj7 x3x45x (C B E).

cards.front: On those C-major shells, how do the upper two notes travel?
cards.back: Strings 3 and 2 move C F, then B F, then B E (frets 5/6 to 4/6 to 4/5). The two guide tones travel at most one fret each time.

cards.front: Write the 12-bar blues in A with seventh chords, bars 1–12, using V7 in bar 12.
Label T, PD, or D for C F G C; C Am Dm G; and C Em F G.
cards.back: T PD D T; T T PD D; T T PD D (iii is a weak tonic in the last).

cards.front: Write ii V I in G, D, and F major.
cards.back: Am7 D7 Gmaj7; Em7 A7 Dmaj7; Gm7 C7 Fmaj7.

cards.front: C F G C versus C F G F: what changed in how the phrase ends?
cards.back: The first ends D to T (V to I), a resolution. The second ends D to PD (V to IV), a retrogression that steps away from the dominant instead of going home.
